overview: Antigua and Barbuda’s history extends from Indigenous island communities to plantation slavery, emancipation and an independent Caribbean state. Archaeological sites preserve evidence of shellfish harvesting, pottery and exchange. Later buildings record the work of enslaved people, while public art and festivals express experiences that continued beyond colonial rule.

periods.title: Shellfish harvesting and exchange on Barbuda
periods.summary: Dated shells from Burton’s Field place activity broadly within these centuries. Excavations along the Strombus Line reveal intensive conch processing and imported flint worked on the island.

periods.title: A long settlement sequence at Indian Creek
periods.summary: Radiocarbon dates indicate extended occupation at Indian Creek on Antigua. Its changing pottery styles became important evidence for the chronology of the island’s Ceramic Age.

periods.title: English colonization and expanding cash crops
periods.summary: English settlers arrived from St. Kitts in 1632. Tobacco, indigo, cotton and ginger preceded the growing dominance of sugar in Antigua’s colonial economy.

periods.title: Plantations and the naval dockyard
periods.summary: Estate processing works and English Harbour’s naval facilities depended on enslaved labor. Their surviving buildings connect sugar production, ship repair and imperial commerce.

periods.title: Emancipation within a plantation society
periods.summary: Slavery ended in 1834, but labor laws and unequal control of resources continued to shape freed people’s lives. Legal freedom did not remove colonial hierarchies.

periods.title: A summer carnival takes shape
periods.summary: Antigua’s annual summer Carnival began in 1957, combining emancipation commemoration with a visitor attraction. Pageantry, calypso and organized street celebrations developed within this festival.

periods.title: Associated statehood
periods.summary: Association with Britain in 1967 preceded full independence. Political change developed alongside the labor movement and debates about the relationship between the islands.

periods.title: An independent state
periods.summary: Antigua and Barbuda became independent on 1 November 1981, with Vere Cornwall Bird as prime minister and Elizabeth II as constitutional monarch.

periods.title: Frank Walter’s place for making art
periods.summary: Walter built a home, studio and garden on Bailey’s Hill. His work encompassed local landscapes, portraits, imagined worlds, writing and music.

periods.title: Recognition of dockyard heritage
periods.summary: The Antigua Naval Dockyard and related archaeological sites entered the World Heritage List. Its interpretation recognizes the skills and labor of enslaved Africans.

items.text: At Indian Creek, pottery from a long-lived settlement helped archaeologists establish a sequence of Ceramic Age styles. Excavations by Irving Rouse, Fred Olsen and Desmond Nicholson in the early 1970s made the site especially influential. The sequence records changes in material culture; pottery categories alone should not be treated as the names of successive nations.

Burton’s Field on Barbuda yielded thousands of whole and broken conch shells, some punctured, alongside flint flakes. Shell samples date activity broadly between about 1400 and 200 BCE. Nearby Cattle Field instead contained many Atlantic pearl-oyster shells. The contrast points to different harvesting activities rather than one uniform island diet.

Flint at the River, Burton’s Field and Cattle Field sites came from outside Barbuda; the researchers considered much of it consistent with Antigua or neighboring Long Island. Outer surfaces and manufacturing debris indicate local knapping of imported stone. Surface alteration prevented reliable use-wear analysis, so the precise task performed by each flake remains uncertain.

At Betty’s Hope, mills, a boiling house and a curing house formed a processing sequence near the cane fields. Water catchments and cisterns supported the estate, while an extensive village for enslaved people lay to the north and west. Reading the layout connects industrial production with residence, surveillance and the labor on which the plantation depended.

Research on food provisioning at Betty’s Hope combines excavated household material with estate correspondence from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Godbout identifies networks reaching Britain, other Caribbean islands and continental America, including informal and illicit trade. The plantation was therefore dependent on supplies and relationships beyond its sugar fields.

English Harbour’s sheltered bays supported ship repair. Enslaved Africans built and operated the dockyard through skilled, coerced labor. The buildings record engineering achievements within an institution defending the plantation economy, making craftsmanship and exploitation inseparable parts of its history.

Dockyard buildings adapted Georgian forms to local conditions. Verandas and storm shutters at the Officers’ Quarters and Senior Officer’s House show how builders modified British designs for the Caribbean climate.

Selvyn Walter recalled how coarse salt from ponds, including Yepton’s near Five Islands village, preserved meat before refrigerators became common. His account connects salt harvesting, household cooking and village livelihoods. It is a recollection of changing food practices, rather than a claim that all households adopted refrigeration at the same time.

Emancipation in 1834 ended legal slavery, but planters sought to maintain their workforce through restrictive legislation. Later union organization and bargaining challenged the imbalance between estate owners and workers. This history places ordinary laborers’ struggles alongside the better-known careers of political leaders.

Barbuda followed a distinct economic path, including fishing, hunting, farming and salvage from shipwrecks. Its Codrington leasehold history differed from the concentration of sugar estates on Antigua. Migration and remittances later connected families abroad with relatives on the island.

The 1957 summer Carnival combined a commemoration of emancipation with organized entertainment. The museum’s published history records business-sponsored floats, a Queen show and a calypso contest at the DeLuxe Cinema. Steelbands and street performances connected musical competition to collective celebration, drawing on older local festivities and wider Caribbean influences.

Frank Walter made landscapes, portraits and abstract compositions on readily available surfaces, including cardboard and the backs of Polaroid photographs. He also carved wood and filled notebooks with poetry, genealogy and musical scores. His practice joined close observation with imagination, using modest materials for a wide-ranging record of Antiguan life and personal thought.

Walter’s work as a photographer and frame maker formed part of his artistic life. In 1993 he built a home, studio and garden on Bailey’s Hill. The Drawing Center’s account connects this working environment to paintings of surrounding landscapes and people, alongside imagined cosmological subjects.

sections.title: Independent government and the islands’ relationship

items.text: Independence on 1 November 1981 ended British colonial rule and created the sovereign state of Antigua and Barbuda within the Commonwealth. Vere Cornwall Bird became its first prime minister. A continuing constitutional monarchy did not mean that the country remained a British colony.

The constitution identifies the Barbuda Council as the island’s principal local-government body. It also provides for a senator appointed on the Council’s advice and special procedures for changing specified local-government provisions. These arrangements give Barbuda a defined institutional place within the shared state, without making its history identical to Antigua’s.

ending.text: British colonial rule ended with independence in 1981. Antigua and Barbuda continues as a sovereign country, while the islands retain distinct local histories and institutions. The older map entries’ endpoints mark changes in the imported layers, not the disappearance of their communities or the end of the modern state.
